user: Why was the line from the external grid outside its limit for longer on 6 January than on 5 January?

grid.name: PGLib IEEE 30-Bus System (Alsac–Stott)
grid.description: Synthetic 7-day profile generated from the bundled PGLib IEEE 30-bus (Alsac–Stott) MATPOWER case: five dispatchable units with their own costs, line ratings from PGLib.

args.symptom: Bus_0 -> Bus_1 [L0] thermal overload persisted longer on 2000-01-06 than 2000-01-05 (measurements, 100% limit).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Demand changes were the principal driver of the overload on both days, with demand driving the longer Jan 6 episode.
hypotheses.finding: Recurring investigation found demand as the main cause in every episode on both days. On Jan 6's sustained 19:15–21:00 episode, demand near the line contributed 59.5% and demand elsewhere 24.4% of the change; Jan 5's 18:30–19:00 episode was also mainly demand-driven (local demand 43.7%).
hypotheses.factor: Demand near Bus_0 -> Bus_1 [L0] (8 buses); Demand elsewhere (13 buses)

hypotheses.hypothesis: Generator output changes explain why the overload lasted longer on Jan 6 than Jan 5.
hypotheses.finding: Generator output was not a consistent explanation for the duration difference: it contributed 16.1% in the Jan 6 sustained event, but on Jan 5 it contributed 38.4% in one event, was ruled out in another, and counteracted the overload in a third. Demand was the main cause across all investigated episodes.

assistant:
The overloaded external-grid branch was **Bus_0 → Bus_1 [L0]**; the other external-grid branch, **Bus_0 → Bus_2 [L1]**, had no overloads on either day.

On Jan 6, L0 exceeded its 100% limit for **10 quarter-hour intervals (2.5 hours in total)**, including a sustained episode from **19:15 to 21:00** that peaked at **134.1%**. On Jan 5 it exceeded the limit for **5 intervals (1.25 hours total)**, peaking at **107.6%**.

The investigations point to **demand as the main driver on both days**. For the sustained Jan 6 episode, demand near L0 accounted for 59.5% of the change and demand elsewhere for another 24.4%. Generation changes contributed in that episode, but they do not consistently explain the longer duration: their effect varied across Jan 5’s episodes. So the evidence points to a stronger, more sustained demand-driven stress on Jan 6—not to a consistent generation-output shift.
